planting.note: Plant grafted saplings in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical lowland climate; seedling trees take longer to bear than grafted stock.

directions: Matoa is a large evergreen tree native to Papua and the Maluku Islands, prized across Indonesia for small, thin-skinned fruit borne in dense hanging clusters that tastes like a cross between lychee, rambutan, and longan. Indonesian growers informally distinguish smooth-skinned 'matoa kelapa' from wrinkled, chewier-skinned 'matoa papeda,' both eaten fresh by peeling and sucking the juicy translucent flesh from the single central seed. Trees require a humid, frost-free tropical climate and deep, well-drained soil, and grafted saplings generally begin fruiting several years sooner than seed-grown trees. Give trees ample room to spread, since the glossy compound leaves cast dense shade and mature specimens become quite large in favorable lowland conditions.
sources: World Agroforestry (ICRAF) — Pometia pinnata species profile
PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) — Fruit species

planting.note: Plant bulb divisions in a warm, humid, frost-free spot in light shade; clumps multiply readily and can be redivided yearly.

directions: Bawang dayak is a clumping bulb plant from Kalimantan used in traditional Dayak herbal medicine rather than as a culinary onion, even though its small bulbs resemble shallots and reveal a striking red-violet flesh when sliced open. Strap-shaped, iris-like leaves grow from offsets that multiply quickly, making division the standard way to propagate established clumps rather than seed. Bulbs are typically dried and steeped as an herbal tea or infused in rice wine for traditional remedies, and plants prefer consistently moist, well-drained soil with protection from both drought and standing water. Allow clumps to establish for four to six months before lifting bulbs for drying.
sources: Journal of Ethnopharmacology — Eleutherine palmifolia ethnobotany studies
Indonesian Institute of Sciences (LIPI) — Kalimantan medicinal plants

planting.note: Scarify hard seed coats before sowing, or plant nursery seedlings in spring in full sun; tolerates poor, dry soils once established but needs frost-free conditions.

directions: Secang is a thorny, small leguminous tree grown throughout Indonesia and Malaysia for its heartwood, which yields the deep red color and fragrant flavor behind the traditional jamu drink wedang secang and older Southeast Asian textile dyes. Trees tolerate poor, dry soils once established and need protection only from frost and prolonged waterlogging, making them easy to grow as a hedgerow or orchard border planting. Branches are periodically coppiced and the inner heartwood chips are dried and boiled to extract color and aroma, with older, denser wood producing a deeper red. Because of its thorny habit, site secang away from high-traffic paths and allow several years of growth before taking the first significant wood harvest.
sources: PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) — Dye and tannin-producing plants
Indonesian Ministry of Agriculture — Biofarmaka Research Center

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and train the climbing vine onto a trellis in a warm, humid, partially shaded spot; it will not tolerate any frost.

directions: Cincau hijau is a climbing vine whose heart-shaped leaves are hand-crushed and kneaded with water to release a natural mucilage that sets into the green jelly used in the popular Indonesian iced drink es cincau hijau. The vine scrambles over trellises or supports in warm, humid, partially shaded locations and is almost always propagated from rooted stem cuttings rather than seed. Regular harvesting of mature leaves encourages flushes of fresh growth, and the plant needs consistently moist soil with no tolerance for chill or frost. Note that the name 'cincau' is also applied to an unrelated black grass-jelly plant, Mesona chinensis, so confirm Cyclea barbata when sourcing planting material.
sources: PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) — Cyclea barbata
Indonesian Center for Agricultural Biotechnology and Genetic Resources Research

planting.note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured palms in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; needs a long hot growing season and a male pollinator or hand pollination for fruit set.

directions: Zaghloul is Egypt's best-known fresh-eating date, grown mainly in the Nile Delta and prized for being harvested and eaten at the crisp khalal stage rather than dried, unlike most commercial dates. The large, elongated fruit turns a vivid red to deep maroon as it matures and has a crunchy texture with a mild, slightly astringent sweetness that Egyptian markets sell for only a few weeks each autumn. Like all date palms it needs a long, hot growing season, deep well-drained soil, and either a male pollinator palm nearby or hand pollination to set fruit reliably. Many years of growth are required before a young palm reaches bearing maturity, so plan for a long-term planting.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture

planting.note: Plant offshoots or tissue-cultured palms in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; fruit is picked soft and fresh rather than dried, so harvest promptly as it ripens.

directions: Hayani is one of the most widely grown Egyptian date cultivars, valued for its soft, almost black fruit that is eaten fresh at the fully ripe rutab stage rather than cured into a dry date. The nearly black skin and soft, juicy, sweet flesh give ripe clusters an appearance closer to black grapes than typical dried dates, and the fruit does not store as long as drier commercial types. Trees need a long, hot growing season, deep well-drained soil, and a male pollinator or hand pollination to set fruit reliably. As with other date palms, expect many years of growth before a young tree reaches bearing age.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture

planting.note: Plant offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained desert-oasis-type soil in full sun; this semi-dry cultivar tolerates intense heat and low humidity better than fresh-eating types.

directions: Siwi is the traditional date of Egypt's Siwa Oasis in the Western Desert, a semi-dry cultivar long relied on for its ability to store well after drying rather than for fresh eating. Its firmer, less perishable fruit has historically been pressed into compact date cakes or boiled down into syrup, making it a staple food-security crop for oasis communities long before refrigeration or export markets existed. The palm tolerates the extreme heat, aridity, and brackish irrigation water typical of Western Desert oases better than softer fresh-eating cultivars. Like other dates it needs a male pollinator or hand pollination and many years of growth before it begins to bear fruit.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture

planting.note: Plant offshoots in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun in Upper Egypt-style hot, dry conditions; this cultivar flowers and ripens earlier than most other date varieties.

directions: Bartamuda is an Egyptian date cultivar grown chiefly in Upper Egypt and valued for ripening earlier than most other varieties, extending the harvest season with the year's first soft, light amber dates well before the main autumn crop comes in. The early flowering and fruit development that give the cultivar its name make it a useful companion planting alongside later-season Egyptian cultivars like Zaghloul and Hayani for growers who want a staggered harvest. Fruit is soft-textured and mild, generally eaten fresh soon after ripening rather than cured for storage. Like all date palms it requires a long hot season, deep well-drained soil, a pollinator source, and many years of growth before first bearing.
sources: FAO Regional Office for the Near East — Date Palm Cultivars
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Date Palm Culture
